segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan Cohort.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea; Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day we put in at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and be cared for.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Putting out from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after sailing across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came down to Myra in Lycia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us aboard it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a good many days we sailed slowly and with difficulty arrived off Cnidus; then, since the wind would not let us go on, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and coasting along it with difficulty we came to a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since a good deal of time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous, because even the Fast had already gone by, Paul advised them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men, I can see that the voyage is going to bring disaster and heavy loss, not only of the cargo and the ship but also of our lives.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and the ship’s owner rather than by what Paul said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since the harbor was unsuitable for wintering in, the majority decided to put out from there, in the hope that they could somehow reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest, and winter there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had achieved their purpose; they weighed anchor and coasted along Crete, close inshore.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But before long a wind of hurricane force, the one called the Northeaster, swept down from the island.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The ship was caught by it and could not head into the wind, so we gave way and were driven along.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to get the ship’s boat under control.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After hoisting it aboard, they used cables to undergird the ship; and fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear and so were driven along.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As we were being violently battered by the storm, the next day they began throwing cargo overboard,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small storm lay upon us, all hope of our being saved was at last being taken away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up among them and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men, you should have listened to me and not put out from Crete, and so been spared this disaster and loss.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now I advise you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, only of the ship.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For last night there stood beside me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I also serve,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar; and look, God has graciously given you all who are sailing with you.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So take heart, men, for I believe God that it will be exactly as I have been told.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But we must run aground on some island.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the fourteenth night came, as we were being driven across the Sea of Adria, about midnight the sailors began to suspect that they were nearing land.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They took a sounding and found twenty fathoms; a little farther on they took another sounding and found fifteen fathoms.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Fearing that we might run aground somewhere on the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the sailors tried to escape from the ship and lowered the ship’s boat into the sea, on the pretext that they were going to lay out anchors from the bow,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Unless these men stay on the ship, you cannot be saved.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it fall away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Until day was about to break, Paul kept urging them all to take some food, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Today is the fourteenth day that you have been waiting in suspense and going without food, taking nothing.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So I urge you to take some food, for this is for your survival; not a hair will perish from the head of any of you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it, and began to eat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they all took heart and took food themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In all we were two hundred seventy-six persons on the ship.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had eaten their fill, they began to lighten the ship by throwing the grain out into the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, and they planned to run the ship ashore on it if they could.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that held the steering oars; then, hoisting the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they struck a place where two seas met and ran the vessel aground; the bow stuck fast and remained immovable, while the stern was being broken up by the pounding.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim away and escape;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the centurion, wanting to bring Paul safely through, kept them from carrying out the plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for land,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the rest to follow, some on planks and some on pieces of the ship. And so it came about that all were brought safely to land.

notes.note: The narrative returns here to the first person plural, last used when Paul arrived in Jerusalem (21:18), and keeps it through the voyage to Rome. The traditional explanation is that the author, or a source he used, was a companion of Paul on the journey. Some scholars regard the 'we' as a literary convention, but that view is a minority one.

A cohort was a unit of several hundred soldiers. 'Augustan' was an honorific title granted to some auxiliary units of the Roman army. A unit with this title appears to have been stationed in the region in the first century, though which one Julius belonged to is not certain.

The Fast is the Day of Atonement, which falls in late September or early October. Ancient sailors regarded the open Mediterranean as dangerous from mid-September and as closed to shipping over the winter. Luke's point is that the safe season had run out.

notes.traditional: lieth toward the south west and north west
notes.note: The Greek says literally that the harbor 'looks along the southwest wind and along the northwest wind'. This may mean it faces those directions, that is, opens to the west. It may instead mean it looks the way those winds blow, that is, toward the northeast and southeast. The identification of Phoenix on the south coast of Crete is disputed, and the choice depends partly on which site is meant.

The best manuscripts give the name Eurakylon, a sailors' compound of the Greek for the east wind and the Latin for the north wind, meaning a wind from the east-northeast. It is translated here because the name tells an English reader nothing. Later manuscripts read Euroclydon, which is the form in the King James Version.

The Syrtis was a stretch of shallows and shifting sandbanks off the coast of North Africa, in the gulfs of modern Libya and Tunisia. Ancient sailors dreaded it. It lay far to the southwest, and a northeast gale would drive a ship straight toward it.

notes.traditional: strake sail (KJV); lowered the sea anchor
notes.note: The Greek word is a general term for equipment, and Luke does not say which piece is meant. It may mean that the crew lowered the mainsail and its yard. It may instead mean that they let out a drag or sea anchor to slow the ship's drift. The translation leaves the term as general as the Greek.

The verb is the one used elsewhere in the New Testament for salvation in the religious sense. Throughout this chapter (also verses 31, 34, 43 and 44) it and its related words refer to rescue from the sea. Many interpreters think Luke means the reader to hear the wider resonance, but the plain sense here is physical survival.

In the first century 'Adria' covered far more than the modern Adriatic. It included the central Mediterranean between Crete and Greece on one side and Sicily and Malta on the other. 'Adriatic' would wrongly place the ship between Italy and the Balkans, so the older form of the name is kept.

notes.phrase: took bread, gave thanks to God
notes.note: Taking bread, giving thanks and breaking it is how any Jewish meal began. It is also the sequence Luke uses for the feeding of the five thousand and the Last Supper. Scholars are divided on whether he intends an allusion to the Lord's Supper here. Most see an ordinary meal described in deliberately familiar language, since the company was largely non-Christian.

A few early witnesses read 'about seventy-six' instead. The difference is very small in Greek and probably arose from a copying slip. The larger number is well within the capacity of an Alexandrian grain ship and is accepted by nearly all editors.

notes.phrase: a place where two seas met
notes.traditional: a place where two seas met
notes.note: The Greek adjective means roughly 'with sea on both sides' or 'between two seas'. It could describe a sandbar or shoal with deep water on either side, a spit of land, or a channel where currents meet. Many modern versions render it 'sandbar' or 'reef'. The translation keeps the more literal phrase because the exact feature is uncertain.

The Greek says literally 'on some of the things from the ship', or equally 'on some of those from the ship'. The second reading would mean that non-swimmers were carried ashore by members of the crew. Most translators take it of wreckage, as here, but the grammar allows either.

candidates.reason: It is rendered both 'serve' and 'worship' across English versions, and readers should see one consistent choice for cultic service to God as distinct from δουλεύω and προσκυνέω.
It covers physical rescue, healing and theological salvation, and a policy is needed on when to keep 'save' and when to use 'rescue' or 'heal', along with σωτηρία and διασῴζω.
It means 'life', 'person' or 'soul' depending on context, and the traditional 'soul' often misleads, so the sense divisions should be fixed once.
It ranges over 'urge', 'encourage', 'comfort' and 'appeal' throughout Acts and the letters and needs sense-by-sense defaults, kept distinct from παραινέω ('advise').
Versions vary between 'Caesar' and 'the emperor', and the choice should be uniform across the Gospels and Acts.
